newsitem.title: INDIA: Success of India, Pakistan talks hinges on secrecy.
newsitem.headline: Success of India, Pakistan talks hinges on secrecy.

text.p: The progress of crucial negotiations between India and Pakistan this weekend will depend on how secret the deliberations are kept by both sides, diplomats said on Thursday.
Talks between senior officials of the two countries broke down in January 1994 after Islamabad raised, and New Delhi resisted, the issue of the disputed Himalayan territory of Kashmir.
"Any high hopes in the media about the imminent success of the talks could be a kiss of death for the future of the dialogue," one senior Western diplomat said.

Diplomats said neither side could budge publicly from their positions since January 1, 1994, when India's then foreign secretary, Jyotindra Nath Dixit, met his then Pakistani counterpart Shaharyar Khan in Islamabad for the last round.
Their current successors, Salman Haidar and Shamshad Ahmad, will lead the four-day talks from Friday.

In 1994, Pakistan publicly insisted the day after talks began that there would be "no further talks with India unless India discusses the status of Kashmir and removes security forces from the Hazratbal shrine," Kashmir's holiest mosque.
The talks broke down on January 3. On January 18, 1994, Pakistan followed up the Khan-Dixit talks with two proposals called "non-papers", both publicly rejected by India.

The papers outlined "modalities" for holding a plebisicite in Kashmir under the supervision of the United Nations and "measures required to create a propitious climate for peaceful resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute and other issues".
The key Pakistani demands included:
* Withdrawal of additional forces deployed in Jammu and Kashmir since 1990.
* Removal of "symbols of the military and paramilitary presence" in Kashmir, especially around the Hazratbal shrine in the state's summer capital of Srinagar.
* Withdrawal of India's anti-terrorist laws.
* End of alleged repression by Indian security forces.
* Release of Kashmiri political and militant leaders.
* Unhindered access to India's Jammu and Kashmir state by human rights bodies and the electronic media.
* Removal of all curbs on travel by Kashmiris out of India.

On January 24, 1994, India handed over a set of six of its own "non-papers" to Pakistan as "outlines of a proposed agreement on the maintenance of peace and tranquility along the line of control (ceasefire line)". All six were rejected by Pakistan.
The Indian proposals included:
* Siachen - Disengagement and redeployment of troops on the Siachen Glacier, the world's highest battlefield.

* Sir Creek - Source of disputed maritime border on the Arabian Sea. India said there was consensus on the land boundary in the region and was prepared to negotiate "around the middle of the Creek along the 1914 resolution map."

* Tulbal (Wullar) navigation project - India said in October 1991 the two sides had finalised a draft agreement on the project on the Jhelum river on the Indian side of Kashmir. It wanted the agreement to be signed as a treaty.
* India-Pakistan Joint Commission - Set up in March 1983 to to promote cooperation in areas of trade, industry, culture, tourism. India proposed a meeting of the commission.

* Confidence Building Measures - In January 1991, India and Pakistan ratified a 1988 Agreement on Prohibition of Attack on Nuclear Installations and Facilities. The sixth Indian proposal sought a pact against the first use or threat to use nuclear capabilities against the other side. It also sought a ban on targeting population centres and economic targets.
Both India and Pakistan both deny having nuclear weapons, but are believed by Western experts to be already in possession or capable of quickly assembling them.
Diplomats said the eight "non-papers" may not figure directly in Friday's talks but a beginning on the core issue of Kashmir could be made if both sides agreed not to go public.
